reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Measured adoption of AI in educational services sits at 30.0% of firms, according to the Census Bureau, down from a prior period figure of 35.5%. That is the only hard adoption number the material offers, and it covers firms in NAICS 61 answering whether they used AI in the last two weeks. The sources do not break that figure down by institution type, so nothing here says whether the decline is concentrated in K-12, higher education, or workforce training.

What the deployments look like comes mainly from the Department of Education, which published federal AI guidance and an inventory of its own use-cases. The Department describes tools including Grammarly for written communication, Otter.AI for real-time transcription and meeting collaboration, AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models, and CAISY for decision-making, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation. Its listed uses are largely administrative and instructional support: generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in multiple programming languages, writing R code for data analysis, extracting key points and action items from public documents, converting data types such as county names into FIPS codes, generating mock datasets for testing, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, and training employees on prompt engineering. The Department also describes testing AI with fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to verify filters and data loss prevention are in place.

On where money and market attention concentrate, HolonIQ is the source the material names, described as a platform for impact market intelligence covering the global impact economy. Its page describes sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, scoring impact with rubrics and ratings, mapping partnership landscapes, and mapping competitive landscapes for governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms, and investors. The sourced points describe HolonIQ as covering EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning. No dollar figures, funding totals, or vendor market shares appear in the material.

The clearest ROI evidence in the excerpts is qualitative and comes from the Department of Education's tool descriptions rather than from measured outcomes. CAISY is said to reduce costs, boost productivity, and support more accurate data-driven decisions by streamlining repetitive tasks. Otter.AI is said to save time and improve accessibility through searchable transcripts. Grammarly is said to improve clarity and tone in written communication. The Department frames its use-case inventory as demonstrating a commitment to AI innovation and advancement, and states that its Office of the Chief Information Officer supports adherence to federal regulations on AI while embracing the technology under the executive order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. No independent ROI study, cost saving figure, or outcome metric appears in the material.

The regulatory posture is set at the federal level for US education through that Department of Education guidance, which the sourced points describe as framing permissible use, risk, and procurement for US schools. The Department's own language ties responsible and secure usage to federal regulation and to the executive order. Beyond that, the material does not describe state-level rules, student privacy statutes, or academic integrity enforcement, even though the page coverage note mentions academic integrity policy from K-12 through university. On the learning side, this site's course catalogue tracks 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, each with one verified source and re-verified daily. It notes that four are university graduate courses, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry sources including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and Andrej Karpathy, and that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few cautious takeaways. Adoption among educational services firms is real but not universal at 30.0%, and it moved down from 35.5% in the prior period, so the sector is not on a uniform upward path. The documented deployments are mostly back-office and instructional-support tasks, drafting, summarizing, transcribing, coding assistance, and data preparation, rather than autonomous teaching. Federal guidance exists and is the named regulatory reference point for US schools, and the Department of Education's own inventory shows what a disclosed, use-case-by-use-case approach looks like. The material does not supply cost benchmarks, vendor pricing, or outcome studies, so any deployment case has to be built on the institution's own evidence rather than on figures reported here.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
